items.title: Bill Crow interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, October 18, 1995
items.q: He loved everything from Louis Armstrong up to about Mugsy Spanier.

ctx.x: So I played that a little bit, didn’t really like it, and didn’t have an opportunity to get into any music on it, because the stuff we were playing, the parts weren’t very interesting. And by this time I’d become interested in jazz. And in high school this same teacher had formed a little swing band, played stocks and was trying to teach us how that idiom went. So I’d bring my baritone horn to rehearsal and say where are the baritone horn parts? And again I was crushed to discover that they didn’t write for that…

had trouble with I wanted everything to be symmetrical, and jazz players have to be able to keep the time going with one hand while they do other things with their other hands. And I always wanted to do things that were symmetrical, and I couldn’t get the asymmetrical things to work right for me. So I eventually gave up drums just by default, but I played them, oh, through high school and in college a little bit. And when I got in the Army, all the drummers in the band I finally got into as a baritone player,…
A moldy fig. I haven’t heard that term in a while.
